store.0: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite challenging, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's amazing to see how much I've grown and how much more I have to learn.

store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by the theory behind real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The class dives into dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending at times. However, our professor is excellent at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She presents a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time and then shows us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with new ideas and insights.

store.4: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, my other challenging class this semester is Distributed Systems(CS 2631). It's a lot of reading and group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with team members who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about the final product. However, this diversity is also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in isolation. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures effectively. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. The professor is from the industry and has worked on a couple of indie games that received some attention. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even exploring user experience design. The assignments are incredibly creative, and I find it unbelievably fun. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. It was challenging to get it right, but it was also rewarding to see the design come together.

store.8: I also have to mention my Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be too advanced for me. However, the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is some math involved, such as linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're exploring basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing to see how these algorithms can solve problems more efficiently. This class has made me rethink how I approach problems and has opened my eyes to the potential of quantum computing.

store.10: My Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all the agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.

store.12: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was a fascinating experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.

store.14: My typical college schedule is quite packed. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload.

store.16: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. Capstone alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it can be even more time-consuming if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the distributed systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated. However, coordinating the schedules of five different people can be a logistical nightmare. Despite the stress it causes, it's also exciting to have these opportunities to fully invest in academic projects without the pressures of a real job environment. It's a chance to learn and explore without any external constraints.

store.18: Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
